entries.content_osis: <div eID="gen30258" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen30259" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen30260" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen30260" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen30259" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen30261" type="x-p"/> This chapter contains two prophecies: the first, delivered during the siege of Jerusalem, predicts to Zedekiah the taking and burning of the city, with his own peaceful death and honorable burial, <reference osisRef="Jer.34.1-Jer.34.7">Jer 34:1-7</reference>. The second was delivered when the Chaldeans had for some time broken up the siege. It reproves the Jews for their conduct towards their brethren of the poorer sort, whom they released, by a solemn covenant, from bondage, in the extremity of their danger; but compelled to return to it when they thought that danger over, <reference osisRef="Jer.34.8-Jer.34.11">Jer 34:8-11</reference>. For this God threatens them with the sword, pestilence, and famine; and with the return of the Chaldeans, who should take the city, destroy it and the other cities by fire, and make an utter desolation of the whole land of Judea, <reference osisRef="Jer.34.12-Jer.34.22">Jer 34:12-22</reference>. <div eID="gen30261" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30262" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen30262" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30263" type="x-p"/> The word which came unto Jeremiah - This discourse was delivered in the tenth year of the reign of Zedekiah. The chapter contains two discourses; one, <reference osisRef="Jer.34.1-Jer.34.7">Jer 34:1-7</reference>, which concerns the taking of the city, and Zedekiah's captivity and death; the other, <reference osisRef="Jer.34.8-Jer.34.22">Jer 34:8-22</reference>, which is an invective against the inhabitants of Jerusalem for having Hebrew male and female slaves. These, having been manumitted at the instance of the prophet, were afterwards brought back by their old masters, and put in the same thraldom; for which God threatens them with severe judgments. <div eID="gen30263" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30264" type="x-p"/> Nebuchadnezzar - and all his army, and all the kingdoms of the earth of his dominion - That is, his army was composed of soldiers gathered out of Babylon, and out of all his tributary dominions: one hundred and twenty provinces.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen30264" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30265" type="x-p"/> He shall burn it with fire - This was a newly-added circumstance. Among many ancient nations they burned the bodies of the more illustrious dead. Odours were used in the burning: they then gathered the ashes, and put them into an urn or pitcher, sometimes into a strong vessel, and buried them. Many of these have been digged up in different parts of England, where the Romans had stations.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen30271" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30272" type="x-p"/> The word that came unto Jeremiah - Here the second discourse begins, which was delivered probably a short time, even a few days, after the former. <div eID="gen30272" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30273" type="x-p"/> Zedekiah had made a covenant - We find no account elsewhere of this covenant: "Every man should let his man-servant and his maid-servant go free;" i.e., as we learn from <reference osisRef="Jer.34.14">Jer 34:14</reference>, on the sabbatical year; for the seventh year was the year of release. See <reference osisRef="Deu.15.12">Deu 15:12</reference>.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen30275" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30276" type="x-p"/> I proclaim a liberty for you - Ye proclaimed liberty to your slaves, and afterward resumed your authority over them; and I had in consequence restrained the sword from cutting you off: but now I give liberty to the sword, to the pestilence, and to the famine, and to the captivity, to destroy and consume you, and enslave you: for ye shall be removed to all the kingdoms of the earth. The prophet loves to express the conformity between the crime and its punishment. You promised to give liberty to your enslaved brethren; I was pleased, and bound the sword in its sheath. You broke your promise, and brought them again into bondage; I gave liberty to the sword, pestilence, and famine, to destroy multitudes of you, and captivity to take the rest. Thus you are punished according to your crimes, and in the punishment you may see the crime. Sword, pestilence, and famine are frequently joined together, as being often the effects of each other. The sword or war produces famine; famine, the pestilence.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen30276" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30277" type="x-p"/> When they cut the calf in twain, and passed between the parts thereof - This was the ancient and most solemn way of making a covenant. <div eID="gen30277" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30278" type="x-p"/> 1. A calf as sacrifice was offered to God to secure his approbation and support. <div eID="gen30278" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30279" type="x-p"/> 2. The victim was then exactly divided from the nose to the rump; the spinal marrow being divided longitudinally, in the most careful manner, that the half of it might remain on each side. <div eID="gen30279" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30280" type="x-p"/> 3. These divided parts were laid opposite to each other, a passage being left between them. <div eID="gen30280" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30281" type="x-p"/> 4. The contracting parties entered this passage at each end, met in the middle, and there took the covenant oath; adjudging themselves to death should they break this covenant. <div eID="gen30281" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30282" type="x-p"/> 5. Then they both feasted on the victim. In reference to this last circumstance, God says he will give their bodies for meat to the fowls of heaven and to the beasts. This is a farther conformity between the crime and the punishment. See my notes on <reference osisRef="Gen.15.9-Gen.15.17">Gen 15:9-17</reference> (note).
